content: The first step involves gathering statistics from individual departmental Morbidity and Mortality (M&M) conferences. The second step is to implement a more formal review process for cases of expired patients through preventable death panel reviews. These reviews can be integrated into multi-departmental evaluations. Such panels typically engage stakeholders from various departments, providing a standardized approach to defining preventability and identifying issues. They also help build consensus on corrective actions, which can foster the political will necessary to implement these actions. For preventable death reviews, autopsy findings can be a valuable source of additional information. While cultural restrictions may limit autopsy use in some regions, it is important to note that significant progress can still be made without autopsy data. However, when available, autopsy reports offer critical insights into the anatomical causes of death, aiding the work of preventable death panels. Autopsies are already conducted for many trauma-related deaths for forensic purposes, with rates exceeding 50% in larger hospitals across Africa, Asia, and Latin America. Given the availability of autopsy reports with precise information on the anatomical causes of death, it is logical to incorporate this data into preventable death reviews and other quality improvement (QI) activities. If the aforementioned methods are already in use, additional steps to consider include tracking audit filters and complications and employing statistical methods for severity adjustment. These approaches provide greater objectivity in identifying problems and more effective means of monitoring the outcomes of corrective actions. These methods rely on the existence of a well-organized source of regular data, which often necessitates the creation of a trauma registry. These considerations can be applied to QI in general, with trauma cases forming a subset of the cases reviewed. However, for hospitals with particularly high trauma volumes (e.g., over 1,000 or 2,000 trauma admissions annually), a dedicated trauma QI program may be warranted due to the specific nature of the problems to be identified and the corrective actions required. For medium-sized hospitals with fewer specialties, many of the above considerations remain applicable, especially if they handle a significant volume of trauma cases. If not, ensuring that trauma cases are adequately addressed within general QI activities, such as M&M conferences, can still yield substantial benefits. The same progression—from preventable death panel reviews to tracking audit filters and complications, and employing statistical risk adjustment methods—applies, depending on trauma volume, local priorities, and resource availability. Smaller hospitals, such as those staffed primarily by general practitioners, and networks of clinics may still find it important to address trauma QI, particularly if they receive a significant number of trauma cases, such as those located along major roads. However, a dedicated trauma QI program may not be justified. Instead, broader management information systems addressing both efficiency and quality improvement across a range of issues are likely to be required. Networks of clinics, smaller hospitals, and medium-sized hospitals often play a critical role in region-wide trauma care, as they frequently serve as the first level of referral to higher-level facilities. In some cases, their role overlaps with prehospital care in the area. Therefore, region-wide efforts to improve trauma care and establish better trauma systems must consider this base of the pyramid of trauma care. Similarly, region-wide trauma QI activities must incorporate cases managed at these facilities. In advanced systems, this can be achieved through the establishment of region-wide trauma registries and formal region-wide trauma QI initiatives. More generally, region-wide preventable death panel reviews could help identify problems in trauma care processes at smaller facilities. Including care providers from these facilities in the panels can help build the political will to implement necessary corrective actions. The specific QI techniques to be utilized at different levels of the healthcare system or in region-wide activities will vary based on local considerations. However, there is almost always a role for improved monitoring of trauma care processes through some form of QI activity at any level of the healthcare system and in any location with significant numbers of trauma patients. When initiating new QI activities or expanding existing ones, two fundamental principles apply at all levels of the healthcare system. The first is to be realistic and build up slowly and sustainably. Taking small initial steps and addressing main priorities, such as obviously preventable deaths, lays the groundwork for long-term success. For example, a hospital with ongoing but relatively ineffective M&M conferences might start by improving the procedural rigor of these conferences and better identifying and following up on corrective strategies. The second principle is to engage and gain the cooperation of a range of stakeholders, including hospital administration, clinicians from various specialties, and, in the case of system-wide QI, prehospital providers and governmental authorities responsible for the area's healthcare network. Any QI activities must have an adequate mandate to gather the necessary information and implement the agreed-upon corrective action plan. Broad political support is equally essential to ensure the success of such corrective actions. This publication provides guidance on implementing QI programs, which are based on participants' knowledge and expertise in clinical trauma care and local standards of best practice. The QI process aims to ensure that local standards are met. While this publication does not address specific clinical issues, determining what standards, clinical guidelines, or algorithms exist, are in place locally, or should be in place locally, is the responsibility of clinicians and administrators in each location. Several resources provide guidance on what constitutes good trauma care, which participants in the QI process may utilize as needed. These include authoritative textbooks on surgery and trauma care, many of which are published in individual countries and tailored to local conditions. For initial management, including resuscitation and diagnostic work-up, several courses outline well-developed care protocols, such as Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS), National Trauma Management Course (NTMC), Primary Trauma Care (PTC), and Trauma Nursing Core Course (TNCC). For prehospital care standards, related courses include International Trauma Life Support (ITLS) and PreHospital Trauma Life Support (PHTLS). Beyond initial management, Definitive Surgical Trauma Care (DSTC) provides protocols for operative management. Additionally, several sets of guidelines may be used to develop individual institutional protocols. For smaller hospitals in lowand middle-income countries, WHO's Department of Essential Health Technology has developed particularly useful references for clinical trauma care. These resources are oriented toward circumstances where resources are limited, and general doctors must perform basic operative care without access to specialists and often with limited referral capabilities. These references include the textbook Surgical Care at the District Hospital and educational materials from the Integrated Management for Emergency and Essential Surgical Care (IMEESC) toolkit, both freely available on the WHO website. These resources provide general guidance on clinical best practices for trauma care and are not exhaustive. Other references may also be useful for QI programs. There is a growing global movement to ensure greater patient safety in healthcare. WHO's Patient Safety Programme, part of the World Alliance for Patient Safety, has worked on initiatives such as the Global Patient Safety Challenges. The first challenge focuses on preventing healthcare-associated infections by promoting better hand hygiene among healthcare workers. The second challenge, Safe Surgery Saves Lives, promotes the use of a standardized surgical safety checklist in operating rooms to prevent errors such as wrong-site surgery and anesthetic complications. This checklist has been pilot-tested in hospitals worldwide and has shown to reduce perioperative complications and mortality. The efforts of the Safe Surgery Saves Lives challenge align closely with the goals of trauma QI, as safe operations are a major component of trauma QI objectives. Similarly, the Joint Commission International (JCI), designated as a WHO Collaborating Centre on Patient Safety, works closely with the World Alliance for Patient Safety. Efforts to promote greater patient safety and trauma QI share several synergies. Both aim to improve information systems to better understand and prevent errors. Both seek to address the challenges of ensuring safety in acute care, where risks are heightened by issues such as staffing constraints and shift work. Most importantly, both efforts strive to change the organizational culture of healthcare institutions to emphasize patient safety and raise political commitment to this goal. Individuals active in either field are encouraged to collaborate, particularly at the local level, to promote changes that will help achieve their mutual objectives. In many institutions, QI for trauma cases is integrated into QI for the entire surgery department or even the entire institution. Only larger institutions with high trauma volumes are expected to have specific trauma QI programs. More broadly, QI for trauma care and other clinical issues is part of overall efforts to strengthen health service management. WHO's Organization and Management of Health Services (OMH) unit, part of the Department of Health System Governance and Service Delivery, has developed resources and training materials for this purpose, freely available on their MAKER website. These materials include references and tools for strengthening health service management, with a section on quality management, including quality assurance, standards, accreditation, user satisfaction, patient safety, and monitoring and evaluation of care quality. While not directly related to trauma QI, these resources offer synergies. Those promoting greater use of trauma QI may find allies within similar movements in primary care and other fields.
